title: 1965 USAF KC-135 Wichita crash
summary: KC-135A Stratotanker took off from McConnell AFB at 9:28 a.m. on 16 January 1965 loaded with 31000 gallons jet fuel. Aircraft gained very little altitude and experienced large yaw. Crew attempted return to airport and dumped fuel. Aircraft made hard left bank and began to enter roll. Unable to recover, crashed into residential neighborhood at Piatt and 20th Street three minutes after takeoff. Impact and resulting explosion destroyed dozens of homes killing all 7 crew and 23 civilians.
probable_cause: Rudder control system malfunction which was impossible for crew to overcome. Parachute ingested into Number 1 engine possibly contributed.

title: LAN Chile 107
summary: LAN-Chile Flight 107, a Douglas DC-6B-404 on a scheduled international flight from Santiago to Buenos Aires, crashed into La Corona Mountain in the Las Melosas area of the Andes at flight level 120 on 6 February 1965, about 1,200 feet below the summit. All 88 occupants were killed, including 22 players and staff of Santiago's Antonio Varas football team traveling to a match in Montevideo. The accident investigation board attributed the crash to the pilot in command choosing a route that followed neither the approved flight plan nor the airline's operations manual, and it ruled that weather was not a factor.
probable_cause: The accident investigation board attributed the accident to the pilot in command, who chose to follow a route that was neither in accordance with the approved flight plan nor the airline's operations manual; weather was not a factor in the crash.

events.text: The DC-6 departed Santiago-Los Cerrillos Airport on the morning of 6 February with 80 passengers and seven crew members bound for Ezeiza, near Buenos Aires.
The pilot in command chose to follow a route that was neither in accordance with the approved flight plan nor the airline's operations manual.
When the aircraft was at flight level 120 in the Las Melosas area of the Andes, it crashed into the side of La Corona Mountain, approximately 1200 ft below its summit; there were no survivors.

title: Eastern Air Lines 663
summary: Eastern Air Lines Flight 663, a DC-7 departing Boston for Atlanta, was executing a Dutch seven departure over the Atlantic when air traffic control detected a potential conflict with Pan Am Flight 212 at a lower altitude. Flight 663 initiated an extreme right turn to avoid collision, but could not recover from the steep bank and plunged into the Atlantic Ocean. All 84 occupants were killed. The CAB determined that evasive maneuvers in dark night conditions with no visible horizon caused spatial disorientation.

title: British United Airways 1030X
summary: British United Airways Flight 1030X departed Paris-Orly for Jersey Airport with 27 passengers and crew. Poor visibility and low cloud cover at Jersey made it difficult to see the runway. The crew aborted the first landing attempt. On the second approach, the aircraft's starboard wing struck the outermost pole of the approach lighting system at 58 feet altitude, 3000 feet short of the runway threshold. The impact severed the starboard wing, the aircraft rolled upside down and caught fire.
probable_cause: The pilot attempted to land in visibility far below that laid down by the airline's procedures. Despite being informed during flight of poor and deteriorating conditions, the pilot elected not to divert to another airport.

title: Pakistan International Airlines 705
summary: PK705 crashed on final approach to Cairo International Airport on 20 May 1965, killing 121 of the 127 aboard. The pilot reported problems with the flaps shortly before the Boeing 720 crashed southeast of the airport and exploded into flames. Investigators found the aircraft did not maintain adequate height for the circuit and continued descending until it contacted the ground; the reason for that abnormal descent could not be determined.

The aircraft crashed southeast of the airport and broke up as it exploded into flames; six passengers were thrown clear of the wreckage but everyone else aboard was killed.

title: United Air Lines 389
summary: The aircraft was cleared to descend to 6,000 feet MSL but never leveled off, continuing its descent at 2,000 feet per minute into Lake Michigan 577 feet below the assigned altitude. Analysis indicated the pilots likely misread their altimeters by 10,000 feet, believing they were at 16,000 feet when actually at 6,000 feet. The first proven case of such an error occurred in 1958.

title: 1965 Hong Kong US Marines KC-130F Crash
summary: A United States Marine Corps Lockheed KC-130F Hercules crashed on takeoff from Kai Tak Airport on 24 August 1965, killing 59 of 71 people aboard. The aircraft veered to the left shortly after takeoff, struck a sea-wall, and plunged into the waters surrounding the runway 40 feet off Hong Kong Island. Investigation attributed the crash to partial failure of the number one engine during takeoff.

title: Pan Am 292
summary: Pan Am Flight 292, a Boeing 707 named Clipper Constitution, departed Fort-de-France on a scheduled flight to New York via Antigua and San Juan with 30 people on board. While on approach to Coolidge Airport in stormy weather, the aircraft at 2,760 feet struck Chances Peak, a 3,002-foot-high mountain on Montserrat. Investigation found the crew made a navigational error and descended below safe minimum altitude while unsure of their position.

title: British European Airways 706 (1965)
summary: British European Airways Flight 706 departed from Edinburgh Turnhouse Airport at 23:17 on 26 October 1965 on a scheduled flight to London Heathrow. During approach to runway 28R with fog reducing visibility to less than 50 metres, the aircraft overshot the runway twice and entered a hold. On the final approach, the crew decided to overshoot with the nose up and reducing flaps. The aircraft crashed 2,600 feet from the threshold and burst into flames. Investigation attributed the crash to pilot error with contributing factors including low visibility, pilot fatigue, anxiety, lack of experience in fog landing, and procedural errors.

title: American Airlines 383
summary: American Airlines Flight 383, a Boeing 727 carrying 57 passengers and 5 crew, was cleared for a visual approach to Cincinnati on November 8, 1965 in deteriorating weather with low visibility. The aircraft descended more rapidly than it should have without either pilot noticing, descending to just 3 feet above the airport while still 3 nautical miles away. The aircraft flew into wooded slopes in the Ohio River valley and crashed. Only three passengers and one flight attendant survived.

title: United Airlines 227
summary: United Airlines Flight 227 crashed short of runway 34L at Salt Lake City while conducting a high and fast unstable approach. The crew descended at approximately 2300 feet per minute, nearly triple the recommended rate, remaining 2000 feet above the normal glideslope at the outer marker. The captain rejected the first officer's attempt to add thrust with only seconds remaining before impact. The aircraft struck the runway with 4.7g vertical acceleration, rupturing fuel lines and causing post-impact fire that turned an initially survivable crash fatal, with 43 killed and 48 survivors.
probable_cause: Captain's bad judgment in conducting the final approach from a position too high and too close to permit descent at normal and safe rate, resulting in impact short of the runway.

title: Aeroflot 99
summary: Tupolev Tu-124 operating scheduled service from Leningrad-Pulkovo to Murmansk descended through poor weather with snow and 1.5 km visibility on 11 November 1965. The pilots, misidentifying neighborhood lights as runway lights, continued descending below the glidepath and increased rate of descent. The aircraft struck frozen Lake Kilpyavr 273 meters short of the approach beacon and 2127 meters short of the runway. 32 of 64 aboard perished; many survivors sustained injuries.
probable_cause: Pilot disorientation and visual illusion from neighborhood lights mistaken for runway lights, combined with descent below the glidepath. Contributing factors included absence of glidepath approach lights and inadequate ATC monitoring of descent rate.
